title: A key-creation endpoint copies the scope the caller asks for instead of intersecting it with the caller's own rights
index_line: T-0056 · AUTH_DECISION · a low-privilege technician mints an API key with administrator scope · java/dotnet/php/python · corroborated
invariant_violated: A scope field on a credential-creation request is assumed to describe what the caller already has, because the UI only offers their own roles. The server treats it as the definition of what the new credential gets. Asking for more is not a privilege escalation in the code's eyes — it is a parameter.

mechanism.does: a user with a low-privilege role calls the API-key creation endpoint directly, bypassing the UI that limited the choices
the request names the permissions the new key should carry
the endpoint validates the requested permissions against the set the product supports, not against the set the caller holds
a key with administrative scope is written to the server's configuration store
the attacker authenticates with their own key and is now an administrator

source.http.request.value: the key-creation request with a permissions array — the escalation is a value in a field, not a missing check

token.claims.value: the scope/permission set attached to the issued credential

guard.none.value: the missing intersection between requested scope and caller scope

sink.file.write.value: the credential store the new key is written into (a config file holding every key and secret)

preconditions.expr: a credential-creation endpoint accepts a caller-supplied scope
an account exists with a role below the requested scope

check.spec: log in with the lowest role available and request the highest scope; a 200 returning a key is the finding

preconditions.expr: the key store holds other principals' secrets, so a wide-scope key reads them

success: a key created by a low-privilege account performs an administrative action
the created key's scope matches what was requested, not what the account held
the key store on disk now contains a credential the caller should not have been able to mint
failure_like: the endpoint intersects requested scope with the caller's effective permissions
keys can only be created by administrators, or scopes are fixed per role
false_positive: a technician who genuinely holds admin via a group — check effective permissions first
a key that is created but rejected downstream: verify an administrative action actually succeeds

hazards: audit every create-a-credential path for the difference between validating the value and validating against the caller
API keys are usually stored beside other secrets, so one over-scoped key is a key-store disclosure
the UI is not a control: enumerate the API behind it with the lowest role you can get
distinct from T-0035 (provisioning trusts an external claim) and T-0046 (no check at all): here a check exists and checks the wrong thing
non_transfers: endpoints that derive scope from the caller's own token rather than from the request body
